items.title: kstack loses deepest frame on function entry when kernel is built with CONFIG_UNWINDER_FRAME_POINTER=y
items.body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

kstack loses the deepest frame when the probe fires at function entry (kprobe) on x86-64.
Example (Linux 6.9, bpftrace 0.21):

```
sudo bpftrace -e 'k:ip_rcv_core { print(kstack); exit(); }'
```
```
ip_rcv_core+1
__netif_receive_skb_list_core+557
```

But the real call chain is:

```
ip_rcv_core+1
ip_list_rcv          ← missing
__netif_receive_skb_list_core+557
```

If we prepend the first 8-byte word at $sp manually we recover the frame:

```
sudo bpftrace -e 'k:ip_rcv_core {
    $lr = *(uint64*)reg("sp");
    printf("        %s%s", ksym($lr), kstack);
    exit();
}'
```

Output:

```
ip_list_rcv          ✓ restored
ip_rcv_core+1
__netif_receive_skb_list_core+557
```

### Root cause

At a kprobe entry the compiler has not yet executed the prologue: %rbp still points to the caller frame, so the first *(rbp+8) the unwinder sees is already one level up. The current function’s LR/return IP lives at *(rsp) until the prologue pushes %rbp and moves %rsp down. Traditional frame-pointer based unwinding therefore skips one layer.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/672265ba-6446-4c80-9943-982c85c085bf)

### Describe the solution you'd like

Augment kstack on x64 so that, when the kprobe/kfentry is at a kernel function entry, and the architecture uses frame-pointer unwinding, we:

1. Read the first 8 bytes at the observed %rsp (on x86-64) and push that IP as frame 0.
2. Continue normal frame-pointer walk starting from %rbp.

### Describe alternative solutions or features you've considered

### codegen: support in-process loading of native objects


Given a position-independent object with simple relocations (no unwind
tables, etc.) we can load this into an executable region and execute
associate symbols. This is a very low-dependency way of supporting the
embedding of host objects/code into both dynamic and AOT bpftrace
programs. The AOT model simple needs the objects embedded in the same
way that it embeds the bytecode, and access to whatever base layer of
runtime functions we want to provide (which could even be different than
the dynamic case, if we wanted to provide this).

This is highly experimental and merely a proof-of-concept.

Signed-off-by: Adin Scannell <amscanne@meta.com>

items.title: tests: use CMake-resolved python3 in runtime-tests.sh
items.body:
`sudo ./build/tests/runtime-tests.sh` fails under a Nix dev shell with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'looseversion'` because sudo strips PATH and PYTHONPATH, so the bare `python3` in `runtime-tests.sh` resolves to `/usr/bin/python3` instead of the Nix-provided interpreter that has the runtime-test dependencies installed.

Make CMake substitute the absolute path of the python3 found at configure time into the generated `build/tests/runtime-tests.sh`, so the launcher always uses the same interpreter regardless of sudo's environment scrubbing. Fall back to a PATH lookup if the placeholder was somehow left unsubstituted or the configured interpreter no longer exists.

This only changes the launcher's interpreter selection; individual test directives that shell out to `python3` are unchanged.

Fixes: https://github.com/bpftrace/bpftrace/issues/5110

## Testing

- `bash -n tests/runtime-tests.sh`
- Simulated CMake substitution of `@Python3_EXECUTABLE@` with an absolute Python path and re-ran `bash -n` on the result.
- Manually checked the fallback paths for configured interpreter present, configured interpreter missing, and source-tree placeholder cases.

I was not able to reproduce the original Nix + sudo environment locally, so reporter/maintainer confirmation would still be helpful.

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.
Currently, bpftrace supports generating userspace stack traces only for programs built with frame pointers. The majority of userspace software is built without frame pointers, making userspace stack traces generated by bpftrace not particularly useful. 

```
ema@ariel:~$ sudo bpftrace -e 'uprobe:/bin/ls:format_user_or_group { print(ustack()) }' 
Attaching 1 probe...
|
        format_user_or_group+0


        0x56141fa17f60


        0x56141fa17f60
[...]
```
<!--
Place description here
-->

### Describe the solution you'd like
<!--

-->
SystemTap supports printing the full userspace stack trace of programs regardless of whether they have been built with frame pointers or not by [using debug information to unwind the user-space stack](https://sourceware.org/systemtap/SystemTap_Beginners_Guide/ustack.html):

items.title: RFC: ustack() with eh_frame information
items.body:
Currently, user mode stack walking (ustack()) relies on frame pointers to be present, which is rarely the case. So ustack() in its current state often produces incomplete stacks.
There are a few tickets related to this:
* https://github.com/bpftrace/bpftrace/issues/1006
* https://github.com/bpftrace/bpftrace/issues/1744
* https://github.com/iovisor/bcc/issues/1234

A possible solution would be to parse the eh_frame/debug_frame sections of the binary and all loaded libs, convert them to tables and push as maps to an eBPF program that does the stack walking.
The tables can be kept pretty compact without sacrificing direkt access to each row, as opposed to walking the full function as in dwarf.
This approach also makes it possible to restore the registers at each frame, giving access to the function arguments. This should be optional, as it comes with a higher runtime cost during stack walking.

This has been done before, for example here
https://www.polarsignals.com/blog/posts/2022/11/29/dwarf-based-stack-walking-using-ebpf
Although they don't restore all registers.

A different solution would be to just copy the user stack and do the walking in user space, as danobi suggested here
https://dxuuu.xyz/stack-symbolize.html. As user stacks can grow pretty large, this approach imho is not feasible for high frequency probes. It also eliminates the possibility to further process the stack inside the probe.

The kernel approach with ORC is also similar.

Upsides:
 * proper stack frames in most environments
 * stack frames with arguments possible

Downsides:
  If the user works in an environment with full frame pointers, using eh_frame information would slow down stack walking. So we should give the user the choice to solely rely on frame pointers.

Implementation:
My idea is to provide the table builder as a standalone library, along with some bpf code, so that it can be used by more than just bpftrace. To find the best way to integrate this into bpftrace I might need some advice/discussion.

The current status is that I have a prototype that works well as a standalone program.

items.title: ustack missing stack frame second from top
8 million ways to die
items.body: Okay, there are only three that I'm aware of: * `LOG(BUG)` seems to be used in some unreachable conditions, more commonly in codegen (86 times). * `assert` is used liberally in codegen and the irbuilder, but also elsewhere (143 times). * runtime exceptions are used mostly in the internals and around tooling (143 times). The coding guidelines recommend the use of exceptions, stating: > If an error is recoverable (meaning downstream callers of the code should be able to selectively handle, ignore, or further propagate), pass the error through the return value of the function. > ... > If an error is not recoverable, prefer throwing FatalUserException. Exceptions should not be used for recoverable errors. There are also 36 try/catch blocks for exceptions. This can be confusing, since there are lots of options to reach from. I would propose the following: * Eliminating unnecessary assertions where possible (e.g. adding -Werror=switch-enum and removing unnecessary `default:` clauses) * Sticking to explicit `assert` statements (with the (portable `&& "this is the error"` style)[https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/error/assert]) for "should never happen" errors * Adding error propagation using a suitable mechanism (e.g. std::optional, llvm::ErrorOr for llvm-bound code, etc.) * Limiting the use of exceptions strictly to high-level runtime errors (in functions that would never conceivable be used transitively in a destructor). That fact that they may throw should be clearly documented (and documented transitively!). Exceptions should be avoided in low-level internals because it is not always clear whether callers would consider it recoverable or not. Practically, I think this means slowly eliminating "LOG(BUG)", as those cases would be forced into one of the above (an assert, error propagation, or very rarely, a runtime exception). I believe that this aligns with the existing coding guidelines against using exceptions if the error is recoverable. None of this is urgent, but I'm filing this bug in order to discuss and ensure that there is consensus. The existing `LOG(BUG)` and exception mechanisms have the following thorny issues: * Exceptions can be thrown from anywhere, and therefore exception safety can be challenging. If exceptions are thrown from a stack unwinding context (e.g. a destructor) then behavior is not defined (and the program is typically immediately terminated). * `LOG(BUG)` uses the destructor for actually emitting the output stream, and therefore cannot be marked `[[noreturn]]` and needs an additional `__builtin_unreachable()` in many cases. It is simpler to avoid this in the first place and jump to the assert. For example, consider the following: ``` if (fd_ < 0) { LOG(BUG) << "fd is less than zero"; __builtin_unreachable(); } close(fd_); ``` Versus: ``` assert(fd_ >= 0 && "fd is valid"); close(fd_); ``` If there is a code path that *can* happen, then this error should be propagated back to the caller anyways (or again, perhaps rarely transformed into a runtime exception if this is a result of a runtime error).

items.title: Dwarf Unwind
items.body:
This is a draft pull request for #4902. It adds dwarf stack unwinding capabilites to bpftrace, see there for more details.

The currently implemented user interface is up for discussion, I'll redo it once we settle on an interface.

I also noticed that I rely on a feature of llvm-21 that is not available in earlier version. I could try to pull the missing bits out of llvm-21 and keep them in bpftrace directly (which might be nasty), or mask the feature for earlier llvm-versions.

Originally I intended the interface between the dwarf-parsing bits and the bpf maps so that the constructed data can be directly streamed into the maps. That requires the support of non-preallocated hash maps, which are rejected on 5.15. So for now I have to collect the data in memory first. I left the restructuring as a separate commit so it can be reverted once the oldest supported kernel is 6.1.

The feature should also be masked for non-x86 platform, although adding support for other platform should be pretty straightforward.

Documentation and tests are also still missing.

items.title: stack broken on kretprobe
Prepare bpftrace for struct arguments to kfuncs
items.body:
BPF is gaining support for [struct fentry arguments](https://lore.kernel.org/bpf/20220812052419.520522-1-yhs@fb.com/). These are currently rejected in the verifier or, if you try to use kprobe, you see the argument split across multiple argX values.

The code from bpftrace 0.15 looks reasonable enough:

```
> bpftrace -dd -e 'kfunc:udp_setsockopt { $tmp = args->optval; }'
...
define i64 @"kfunc:udp_setsockopt"(i8* %0) section "s_kfunc:udp_setsockopt_1" {
entry:
  %"$tmp" = alloca i64, align 8
  %1 = bitcast i64* %"$tmp" to i8*
  call void @llvm.lifetime.start.p0i8(i64 -1, i8* %1)
  store i64 0, i64* %"$tmp", align 8
  %2 = ptrtoint i8* %0 to i64
  %3 = bitcast i8* %0 to i64*
  %4 = getelementptr i64, i64* %3, i64 3
  %optval = load volatile [16 x i8], i64* %4, align 1
  %5 = ptrtoint [16 x i8] %optval to i64
  store i64 %5, i64* %"$tmp", align 8
  ret i64 0
}
```
(This code blows up at the assertion [here](https://github.com/iovisor/bpftrace/blob/master/src/ast/irbuilderbpf.cpp#L1117) in debug builds.)

Interestingly, this 16 byte copy is kinda correct. However, semantically, it produces a value that cannot be used. Namely, the type of `$tmp` is an anonymous struct (`typedef sockptr_t`) with unnamed members (a union), so it cannot be passed to `buf`, `str`, `printf`, or `print` directly. `->` navigation also doesn't work because it's not a pointer to a struct. 

I'm opening this issue to discuss what the language semantics for these values should be. 

I am of the opinion that $tmp in the above program should magically become pointer-to-struct, so everything works transparently but maybe that's too much magic.

I'm also interested to hear if we think this is worth solving for kprobe programs as well. (It *can* be, it's just more complexity).

items.title: CI: do not build ASAN for LLVM <=16
items.body:
While working on #3772, I ran into what looks like a memleak in older LLVM versions.

It looks like LLVM versions <=16 contain a memleak in `DIBuilder` which only manifests when creating debug info for kfuncs. We now only have a single kfunc (`bpf_map_sum_elem_count`) which is only used for LLVM >=17 so the issue did not appear, yet, however, adding new kfuncs will trigger it.

It looks like this is a bug in older LLVM versions so the simplest thing for us is to disable ASAN on these versions.

This adds a new CI env variable `BUILD_ASAN` (turned on by default) which allows to disable ASAN for specific jobs.

I'm wondering if it makes sense to implement parsing of debug information from binaries.
 
Being able to do so would improve the experience of tracing (not only) userspace programs. Examples of features that would be possible:
- accessing (and printing) `uprobe` arguments by name (issue #1742)
- no need to include userspace headers to access struct fields
- `uprobe:line-number` probes (issue #1743)

### Describe the solution you'd like
<!--

-->

Implement support for debug information. While DWARF seems to be the default choice, its support may have some downsides (at the very least introducing a new dependency on a parser library). As an alternative, we could support at least parsing of BTF for userspace programs, which shouldn't introduce any additional dependencies.

Has this been discussed before? Any opinions on this?

items.title: Prefer static types over double dynamic dispatch
items.body:
Currently, the visitor used for all the AST validation, rewriting and code
generation has two separate layers of virtual function indirection (and
occasionally makes use of a manually-crafted vtable-like hashtable keyed by the
RTTI typeids for hand-rolled dynamic dispatch). This is more complex than
necessary, and limits the opportunities for the compiler to optimize these
passes by e.g. folding a visitor into only the things that it actually cares
about visiting.

This change is intended to be non-functional, and makes use of the C++
Curiously Recurring Template Pattern (CRTP) to make each visitor implementation
fully non-virtual and self-contained. This commit does not quite eliminate the
need for RTTI at all, which is left to a subsequent change just to keep each
commit manageable. The `Expression*` and `Statement*` types now have explicit
types that are dispatched, which will be subsequently eliminated.

This is a follow-on from https://github.com/bpftrace/bpftrace/pull/3698.

##### Checklist

- ~~[ ] Language changes are updated in `man/adoc/bpftrace.adoc`~~
- ~~[ ] User-visible and non-trivial changes updated in `CHANGELOG.md`~~
- ~~[ ] The new behaviour is covered by tests~~

items.title: Replace 'bpf_get_stackid'
items.body:
The native `bpf_get_stackid` function is broken by design.

First, stacks can suffer from hash collisions and we can lose stacks.
We receive collision errors in userspace b/c we do not set
BPF_F_REUSE_STACKID.

Second, there is not a great way to reduce the frequency of collision
(other than increasing map size) b/c multiple probes can be sharing
the same stack (remember they are hashed). As a result, we cannot
delete entries in this map b/c we don't know when all the sharers
are gone.

This diff implements our own get_stack_id function utilizing the
quick hash function murmurhash2:
https://github.com/aappleby/smhasher/blob/92cf3702fcfaadc84eb7bef59825a23e0cd84f56/src/MurmurHash2.cpp

This involves:
- creating a scratch map (the stack is too large as a stack var)
- calling `bpf_get_stack` to populate the stack
- calling `murmur_hash_2_func_` to get the stack id
- storing the stackid and stack as a key/value in a hash map

More details:
https://github.com/bpftrace/bpftrace/issues/2962

items.title: Improve codegen for 32-bit architectures
items.body:
This is a follow-up to #2360. The main issues I've run into on armv7 have to do with pointers in bpftrace being 64-bit, which results in misaligned loads and/or wrong offsets; for example:
```
# bpftrace -ve 't:syscalls:sys_enter_open { printf("%p\n", args->filename); }'
0: (b7) r2 = 0
1: (7b) *(u64 *)(r10 -16) = r2
2: (79) r2 = *(u64 *)(r1 +12)
invalid bpf_context access off=12 size=8
``` 
(individual commit messages go into more details)

This changeset tackles this by modifying the size of ctx-relative pointer loads and `bpf_probe_read` calls so it depends on the target arch (4 bytes on armv7, unchanged on all other supported architectures) and adjusting ctx offsets when reading register values.

items.title: Switch development to llvm12
items.body:
As @Birch-san  raised in https://github.com/iovisor/bpftrace/discussions/1785 and https://github.com/iovisor/bpftrace/discussions/1782 our development proces is a bit annoying. 

With the release of LLVM12 I think its time to update our dev setup to LLVM12 only. Most distros have already moved away from llvm7 and 8-11 have the stack reuse bug so 12 seems like our best option.

I don't think we really need to test all these versions, our codegen is still pretty much the same between all versions. We might have a API rename, but no completely different logic.

That would mean our codegen and codegen validator tests would be LLVM 12 only. Support for all other versions can be dropped (just don't run the tests).

It's a bit of churn but afterwards we can ignore it again for 1.5/2y (hopefully)

@danobi @Birch-san @olsajiri @viktormalik  thoughts?

items.title: kprobe arguments
items.body:
This depends on #31. One of these should work:

```
bpftrace -e 'kprobe:do_nanosleep { printf("expires %lld\n", arg0->_softexpires); }'
bpftrace -e 'kprobe:do_nanosleep { printf("expires %lld\n", ((struct hrtimer_sleeper *)arg0)->_softexpires); }'
```

Or both. The first, where the kernel is self-aware of the arg0 type, may depend on the presence of BTF or debuginfo. In their absence, with kernel headers only, it may be required to specify the type.

This is likely a significant amount of work, and may involve sources struct information from these locations, if any are present:

- kernel headers
- kernel debuginfo
- BTF
